task-scheduler.d: Run CPU tasks (letters) so that identical tasks are at least n intervals apart; idle slots are allowed. Return the minimum number of intervals.
task-scheduler.ex: [A,A,A,B,B,B], n=2 -> 8 (A B idle A B idle A B)
task-scheduler.i: Simulate with a max-heap of remaining counts and a cooldown queue of (count, readyTime): always run the most frequent available task. Formula: max(len, (maxFreq - 1) * (n + 1) + #tasks with maxFreq).

time-based-key-value-store.d: Design set(key, value, timestamp) and get(key, timestamp), which returns the value with the largest timestamp <= the given one ("" if none).
time-based-key-value-store.ex: set(foo,bar,1); get(foo,3) -> bar; set(foo,bar2,4); get(foo,4) -> bar2
time-based-key-value-store.i: Map key -> list of (timestamp, value), already sorted because timestamps only increase. get is a binary search for the last timestamp <= t.
k: HashMap of lists + upper-bound binary search

top-k-frequent-elements.d: Return the k most frequent elements.
top-k-frequent-elements.c: n <= 1e5, better than O(n log n)
top-k-frequent-elements.i: Count with a map. Bucket sort by frequency (index = count, at most n) and read buckets from high to low: O(n). A heap is O(n log n), or O(n log k) with a size-k min-heap.

trapping-rain-water.d: Given bar heights, compute how much rain water is trapped between them.
trapping-rain-water.i: Water at i = min(maxLeft[i], maxRight[i]) - h[i]. Prefix/suffix max arrays give O(n) space. Two pointers give O(1): always move the side with the smaller max, since that max bounds the water there.

triangle.d: Return the minimum path sum from the top to the bottom of a triangle, stepping to index i or i+1 on the next row.
triangle.i: Go bottom-up: dp[j] = tri[i][j] + min(dp[j], dp[j+1]) starting from the last row. dp[0] is the answer, using O(n) space.

two-sum.d: Return the indices of the two numbers that add up to target (exactly one solution).
two-sum.i: One pass with a HashMap value -> index: for each x, if target - x has been seen, you're done; otherwise store x.

two-sum-ii-input-array-is-sorted.d: In a sorted array, return the 1-based indices of two numbers summing to target, using O(1) extra space.
two-sum-ii-input-array-is-sorted.i: Two pointers from both ends: if the sum is too big move right left, if too small move left right.

unique-paths.d: A robot moves only right or down on an m x n grid. Count the paths from the top-left to the bottom-right.
unique-paths.i: paths(i, j) = paths(i-1, j) + paths(i, j-1), with the first row and column all 1. Math shortcut: C(m+n-2, m-1).

unique-paths-ii.d: Unique Paths, but some cells are obstacles that can't be used.
unique-paths-ii.i: Same recurrence, but an obstacle cell has 0 paths. Be careful with the first row and column: after an obstacle, the rest of that row or column is 0.

valid-anagram.d: Return whether t is an anagram of s.
valid-anagram.i: An int[26] count: increment for s, decrement for t, then check all zeros. For Unicode, use a HashMap.

valid-palindrome.d: After lowercasing and dropping non-alphanumeric characters, does the string read the same both ways?
valid-palindrome.ex: "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" -> true
valid-palindrome.i: Two pointers from both ends, skipping non-alphanumerics and comparing lowercase characters. No need to build a cleaned copy.

valid-parentheses.d: Return whether a string of ()[]{} brackets is properly matched and nested.
valid-parentheses.i: Push openers onto a stack. On a closer, the top must be its matching opener (pop); otherwise it's invalid. Valid only if the stack is empty at the end.

valid-parenthesis-string.d: A string has '(', ')' and '*' where '*' can be '(', ')' or empty. Is it a valid parentheses string?
valid-parenthesis-string.i: Greedy range: track the min and max possible number of open brackets. '(' adds 1 to both, ')' subtracts 1 from both, '*' does lo-1 and hi+1. If hi < 0, fail; clamp lo at 0. Valid if lo == 0 at the end.

valid-sudoku.d: Check whether the filled cells of a 9x9 board break any Sudoku rule (rows, columns, 3x3 boxes).
valid-sudoku.i: Nine HashSets each for rows, columns and boxes. The box index is (r/3)*3 + c/3. A repeated digit in any set means invalid.

validate-binary-search-tree.d: Return whether a binary tree is a valid BST (strict ordering).
validate-binary-search-tree.c: <= 1e4 nodes, values span the full int range
validate-binary-search-tree.i: Pass down an allowed (min, max) range; every node must lie strictly inside it. Use long bounds because node values can equal Integer.MIN/MAX. (Inorder must be strictly increasing is the alternative.)
k: DFS with (min, max) bounds as long

vertical-order-traversal-of-a-binary-tre.d: Group nodes by column (left to right); within a column order by row, then by value for ties.
vertical-order-traversal-of-a-binary-tre.i: BFS or DFS recording (col, row, val). Use a TreeMap<col, TreeMap<row, PriorityQueue<val>>> so everything comes out sorted.

word-break.d: Can s be split into a sequence of dictionary words (reuse allowed)?
word-break.i: dp[i] = true if some word matches s starting at i and dp[i + len] is true; dp[n] = true. Fill from right to left (or memoise the recursion).

word-ladder.d: Return the number of words in the shortest sequence from beginWord to endWord where each step changes one letter and every word is in the list, or 0.
word-ladder.i: BFS over words. For each position try all 26 letters; if the new word is in the set, enqueue it and remove it from the set (that marks it visited).

word-search.d: Can word be traced in the grid through adjacent cells without reusing a cell?
word-search.i: DFS backtracking from each matching start cell. Mark the cell as used (e.g. temporarily change it), recurse in 4 directions, then restore it.
k: DFS, mark by mutating the board
DFS with a HashSet of used cells

word-search-ii.d: Return every word from a list that can be traced in the grid (adjacent cells, no reuse within a word).
word-search-ii.i: Insert all words into a trie, then DFS from every cell, moving down the trie in step with the path. Prune as soon as the prefix isn't in the trie. Record words at end nodes.
